items.note: Udayagiri cave 20 (Parshvanatha) near Vidisha: eight-line inscription dated Gupta Era 106, A.D. 272.
Udayagiri caves 6 and 7 contain Gupta-period inscriptions; cave 6 bears an inscription of Chandragupta II dated Gupta Era 82.
Tawa cave inscription: cave made by a minister of Chandragupta, dedicated to Shambhu or Siva; inscription undated.
Udayapur described as once a place of considerable importance, now a large village in Basoda Tahsil.
Gazetteer location: nearest station Bareth 6.5 km west; Basoda about 13 km; about 55 km north-east of Vidisha.

claim.value: about 55 km NE of Vidisha, 13 km from Basoda, Bareth station 6.5 km to the west

items.note: Traces of an old fortification wall of great uncemented stone blocks extending to a rocky hill about one km south of the village.
One of the old Sanskrit inscriptions says Udayapura was founded by the Paramara king Udayaditya in the latter half of the 11th century and that he built a Siva temple named Udayeshwara.

claim.value: founded by Paramara Udayaditya, latter half of 11th century A.D.

items.note: Two other inscriptions refer to temple construction commencing in Vikrama Samvat 1116, A.D. 1059.
Flag-staff erected VS 1137, A.D. 1080; records show temple built by order of Udayaditya between A.D. 1059 and 1080.
Temple stands in a spacious square courtyard within a dwarf compound wall, outer face carved, inner face with a line of back-rest seats.
Entrance steps guarded by door-keepers; of eight attendant shrines only six stand in ruin; main temple has shrine room, hall and three entrance porches.
Large lingam covered with a brass sheet presented by a general of Mahadji Sindhia in 1775, as recorded in a contemporary record.

claim.key: brass cover of the liṅga: donor

items.note: Pillars and seats in the three porches are engraved with numerous Sanskrit inscriptions and a few pilgrims' records, some historically important.
Exterior adorned with Brahma, Vishnu, Ganesha, Kshetrapalas; Siva and Durga predominant.
Spire tall and beautifully designed, hall and porches pyramidal-roofed; spire decorated with miniature repetitions in vertical ribs and medallions.
Muhammad Tughluq, A.D. 1336-38, damaged the attendant temples and built a mosque behind the temple from their material; two Persian inscriptions record it.
Fine example of Indo-Aryan style; sculpture style closely resembles Khajuraho, ornamental motifs finer in places.

claim.value: Indo-Aryan style, close to Khajuraho sculpture

items.note: Udayaditya's inscription says he excavated a tank named after him, Udayasamudra, ruins of which lie a short distance away.

claim.value: tank excavated by Udayaditya, ruins seen at a short distance

items.note: Bijamandal or Ghadiyalan-ka-makan, probably contemporary with the temple; name suggests a house for a time-keeper; incomplete Sanskrit record opens with praise to the Sun-god.
Barakhambi is part of a temple built in the 11th century A.D., on the outskirts of the village.
Barakhambi hall: raised seats with back rests and a ceiling of a massive slab.
Pisanari-ka mandir traditionally said built by a woman from her earnings grinding flour for the workmen of the Udayeshwara temple; gazetteer says the building is architecturally of much later date.
Shahi-masjid: Persian inscription says work began under Jehangir and finished under Shahjahan in A.D. 1632.
Remains of a palace or mansion, probably the local governor's residence, in simple early Mughal style with good stone jali work.

claim.value: not named; probably the local governor's residence (early Mughal style)

items.note: Ruins of a small mosque outside the eastern gate of the wall, Mandu-style, built by an agent of Sherkhan under Ghias Shah Khilji in A.D. 1488 per Persian and Sanskrit inscriptions.
Ghod-daud-ki-baodi with wide steps down which horses could run; nearby rock sculptures including an unfinished image and a Sapta Matrikas panel.
Village area about 1,966 hectares; population given as 928 in 1901 and 2025 in 1971 (text also prints 1619 for 1901, apparently an error).
Inscription of Paramara Udayaditya from Udayapur, dated 1173 A.D. as printed.
It names the surrounding district Bhailasvamin of ten sub-divisions including Bhringarika of 64 villages, under a Dandanayaka probably headquartered at Udayapur.
Tabaqat-i-Nasiri: Muhammadans destroyed a great temple of this region; probably the Bhillasvami temple at Bhilsa.
Under the Mughals Bhilsa was reduced to a mahal headquarters; Aurangzeb tried unsuccessfully to rename it Alamgirnagar.
Bijamandal mosque at Bhilsa built by Aurangzeb in 1682 from the material of an 11th-century Hindu temple.
